excerpt: The following mitigation process for external deployments will be applied to models reaching a misuse T/CCL, allowing for iterative and flexible tailoring of mitigations to each risk and use case.
paraphrase: This deployment mitigation process applies to models reaching a misuse T/CCL and allows flexible, iterative tailoring.

excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
paraphrase: Safeguards and risk assessments are developed through an iterative process described below.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability, which may include measures such as safety post-training, monitoring and analysis, account moderation, jailbreak detection and patching, user verification, and bug bounties.
paraphrase: Safeguards targeting the capability may include post-training, monitoring, moderation, jailbreak defenses, user verification, and bug bounties.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through testing (e.g. automated evaluations, red teaming) and threat modeling research. This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
paraphrase: Mitigation robustness is assessed via testing and threat modeling, considering several factors.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The effectiveness of the mitigations. For example, tests run on mitigated models may suggest that the refusal rate and jailbreak robustness together imply that threat actors are unlikely to be able to circumvent safeguards.
paraphrase: One factor is mitigation effectiveness, such as evidence from refusal rate and jailbreak robustness testing.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The likelihood and consequences of model misuse, capability improvements after the risk assessment, and likelihood and consequences of our mitigations being circumvented, deactivated, or subverted.
paraphrase: Another factor is the likelihood and consequences of misuse, capability change, and mitigation failure.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The scope of the deployment. For example, small scale and private deployments may pose substantially less risk than large scale or public deployments.
paraphrase: Deployment scope, such as scale and privacy, is another factor considered.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: What capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models. For example, whether another (non-Google) publicly deployed model is at the same T/CCL, and has mitigations that are less effective at preventing misuse than that of the model being assessed, in which case the deployment of this model is less likely to materially increase risk.
paraphrase: A further factor is comparison to capabilities and mitigations available on other public models at the same threshold.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The historical incidence and severity of related events: for example, whether data suggests a high (or low) likelihood of attempted misuse of models at the T/CCL. Mitigations would consequently have to be stronger (or would not have to be so strong) for deployment to be appropriate.
paraphrase: Historical incidence and severity of related events inform how strong mitigations must be.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Where the model has reached a CCL, the residual risk assessment will be supplemented with a safety case.
paraphrase: If a model reaches a CCL, a safety case supplements the residual risk assessment.

excerpt: Pre-deployment review of residual risk assessment: external deployments of a model take place only after the appropriate governance function determines the residual risk to be acceptable (including a safety case where a CCL has been reached).
paraphrase: External deployment occurs only after governance approval of the residual risk assessment, including a safety case if applicable.

context_stem: Pre-deployment review of residual risk assessment
excerpt: In particular, we will deem deployment mitigations adequate if the evidence suggests that for the T/CCLs the model has reached, the increase in likelihood of harm from the proposed external deployment has been reduced to an acceptable level.
paraphrase: Mitigations are deemed adequate if evidence shows the harm-likelihood increase has been reduced to an acceptable level.

excerpt: Post-deployment processes: our residual risk assessments, safety cases and mitigations may be updated as a result of post-market monitoring, including information about incidents relating to our frontier safety risk domains.
paraphrase: Post-deployment monitoring may lead to updates of risk assessments, safety cases, and mitigations.

excerpt: Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review and might result in updates to the related residual risk assessment or safety case.
paraphrase: Material safety case updates go to governance for review and may prompt further updates.

excerpt: This process is designed to ensure that residual risk remains at acceptable levels: evidence of efficacy collected during development and testing, as well as expert-driven estimates of other parameters, will enable us to assess residual risk and to detect substantial changes that invalidate our risk assessment.
paraphrase: The process aims to keep residual risk acceptable using efficacy evidence and expert estimates to detect invalidating changes.

excerpt: With iteration on mitigations and residual risk assessments, we believe that we are able to make informed decisions about the level of risk via a T/CCL before a model is deployed, and prevent models posing unacceptable levels of risk from being deployed.
paraphrase: Iteration on mitigations and assessments is believed to enable informed risk decisions and prevent deployment of unacceptably risky models.

excerpt: See section 5 of https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01849.
paraphrase: A footnote points to section 5 of an external paper.

excerpt: While we monitor for potential future risks related to insider misuse, our current assessment of these risk domains indicates that the risks of insider misuse posed by the misuse T/CCLs identified below are effectively addressed by our baseline controls (such as background checks and access restrictions).
paraphrase: Insider misuse risks for the listed misuse T/CCLs are currently assessed as adequately addressed by baseline controls.

excerpt: At this stage, additional mitigations beyond these established safeguards are not required.
paraphrase: No additional mitigations beyond baseline controls are currently required for insider misuse.

excerpt: We set out below a set of CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation CCLs as well as the CBRN TCL that we have identified through ongoing analysis of these risk domains.
paraphrase: The document presents CCLs for CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation, plus the CBRN TCL, from ongoing analysis.

excerpt: We expect these to evolve over time.
paraphrase: These capability levels are expected to change over time.

excerpt: We recommend a security level for each CCL, which reflects our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
paraphrase: A recommended security level for each CCL reflects the assessed minimum appropriate security for the field.

excerpt: In practice, our overall security posture may commonly exceed the baseline levels recommended here.
paraphrase: Actual security practice often goes beyond the recommended baseline levels.

excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking proportionate to the risks posed and may be adjusted if our understanding of the risks changes.
paraphrase: Recommended security levels are proportionate to current risk understanding and may be revised.

excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other publicly available models that have weaker security applied (in which case the marginal benefit of higher security is limited), or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Adjustment may occur if the model is not meaningfully more capable than weaker-secured public models, or if open release benefits outweigh risks.

excerpt: Relatedly, we believe these recommendations will only be effective if the entire frontier AI field applies them, and of limited social utility if not.
paraphrase: The recommendations are believed effective only if adopted field-wide, otherwise of limited value.

excerpt: This risk domain focuses on risks of models assisting in the development, preparation and/or execution of a CBRN threat.
paraphrase: The CBRN domain covers model assistance in developing, preparing, or executing CBRN threats.

section_heading: Table 2.2.1.a: CBRN CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.1.a / CBRN uplift level 1 / Critical Capability Level
context_stem: Row: CBRN uplift level 1; Column: Critical Capability Level
excerpt: CBRN uplift level 1: Provides low to medium resourced actors uplift in reference scenarios resulting in additional expected harm at severe scale.
paraphrase: CBRN uplift level 1 is defined as providing low-to-medium resourced actors uplift causing additional expected harm at severe scale.

section_heading: Table 2.2.1.a: CBRN CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.1.a / CBRN uplift level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: CBRN uplift level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: Security level 2+ The difficulty of building defenses against certain CBRN threats means the exfiltration, unauthorized modification, and leak of model weights with this capability could be highly damaging.
paraphrase: Security level 2+ is recommended because CBRN threats are hard to defend against, making weight exfiltration highly damaging.

section_heading: Table 2.2.1.a: CBRN CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.1.a / CBRN uplift level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: CBRN uplift level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: However, the low to medium resourced actors who would be likely to experience the most CBRN uplift are unlikely to pose a substantial exfiltration threat at the level of OC3 groups as defined by RAND.
paraphrase: Low-to-medium resourced actors most likely to gain uplift are unlikely to pose an exfiltration threat at the level of RAND's OC3 groups.

context_stem: The CBRN TCL is defined as follows:
excerpt: CBRN uplift TCL: Provides low to medium resourced actors uplift in reference scenarios, resulting in material risk of CBRN attacks that could result in significant but not severe harm.
paraphrase: The CBRN TCL is defined as providing uplift to low-to-medium resourced actors, creating material risk of significant but not severe harm.

excerpt: Here, and in other misuse T/CCLs, we intend this to mean relative to a baseline without generative AI.
paraphrase: The additional-harm concept is defined relative to a baseline without generative AI.

excerpt: This risk domain focuses on risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
paraphrase: The cyber domain covers model assistance in developing, preparing, or executing cyber attacks.

section_heading: Table 2.2.2.a: Cyber CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.2.a / Cyber uplift level 1 / Critical Capability Level
context_stem: Row: Cyber uplift level 1; Column: Critical Capability Level
excerpt: Cyber uplift level 1: Provides sufficient uplift with high impact cyber attacks for additional expected harm at severe scale.
paraphrase: Cyber uplift level 1 is defined as providing sufficient uplift for high-impact cyber attacks causing additional severe-scale harm.

section_heading: Table 2.2.2.a: Cyber CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.2.a / Cyber uplift level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: Cyber uplift level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: Security level 2+ Models able to greatly assist cyber attack might be of interest to well-resourced state actors.
paraphrase: Security level 2+ is recommended since highly capable cyber-assisting models could attract well-resourced state actors.

section_heading: Table 2.2.2.a: Cyber CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.2.a / Cyber uplift level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: Cyber uplift level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: However, the potential for automated cyber-defense and social adaptation as a response to exfiltration means that higher levels of security, and the resulting costs to innovation, are likely not warranted.
paraphrase: Automated cyber-defense and social adaptation mean higher security levels, with their innovation costs, are likely unwarranted.

excerpt: This risk domain focuses on risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
paraphrase: The harmful manipulation domain covers risks from misuse of highly manipulative models causing large-scale harm.

excerpt: Note: The research into harmful manipulation from a severe risk perspective is nascent. The CCL and our assessment of the risk in this domain is exploratory and subject to further research, and may be substantially changed over time.
paraphrase: Research on harmful manipulation is nascent, and the associated CCL is exploratory and subject to future substantial change.

section_heading: Table 2.2.3.a: Harmful Manipulation CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.3.a / Harmful manipulation level 1 / Critical Capability Level
context_stem: Row: Harmful manipulation level 1 (exploratory); Column: Critical Capability Level
excerpt: Harmful manipulation level 1 (exploratory): Possesses manipulative capabilities sufficient to enable it to systematically and substantially change beliefs and behavior in identified high stakes contexts over the course of interactions with the model, reasonably resulting in additional expected harm at severe scale.
paraphrase: Harmful manipulation level 1 is defined as capability to systematically and substantially change beliefs and behavior in high-stakes contexts, resulting in severe-scale harm.

section_heading: Table 2.2.3.a: Harmful Manipulation CCL and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 2.2.3.a / Harmful manipulation level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: Harmful manipulation level 1 (exploratory); Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: Security level 2+ The lower velocity of harm scenarios associated with this CCL and the viability of social defenses against large-scale misuse of such models count against security mitigations with substantial costs to innovation.
paraphrase: Security level 2+ is recommended because slower harm scenarios and viable social defenses argue against costly innovation-impacting mitigations.

section_heading: Section 3: Machine Learning R&D and Misalignment
excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of significant or severe harm through machine learning R&D and misalignment, and then details our set of TCL and CCLs, as well as the mitigations that we provisionally assess as appropriate for them.
paraphrase: The section outlines the mitigation approach and defines TCL/CCLs and associated provisional mitigations for ML R&D and misalignment risks.

excerpt: As with misuse T/CCLs, we take a similar approach to security and deployment mitigations for ML R&D and Misalignment T/CCLs, although deployment mitigations focus on different threat models and therefore also include measures for high-risk internal deployments.
paraphrase: ML R&D and misalignment T/CCLs follow a similar mitigation approach to misuse, but also cover high-risk internal deployments due to different threat models.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration and unauthorized modification risk are important for models reaching ML R&D CCLs.
paraphrase: Security measures against exfiltration and unauthorized modification are important once ML R&D CCLs are reached.

excerpt: In addition, exfiltration of highly capable models increases the likelihood they will be misused to achieve other critical capabilities, or deployed without adequate control and oversight.
paraphrase: Exfiltration of highly capable models raises the risk of misuse toward other critical capabilities or ungoverned deployment.

excerpt: Below, we rely again on security levels to articulate the security goal recommended for each CCL.
paraphrase: Security levels are again used to state the recommended security goal for each CCL.

excerpt: Security mitigations also protect against the risk of the model exfiltrating itself.
paraphrase: These security mitigations also guard against a model self-exfiltrating.

excerpt: The following mitigation process will be applied for deployments of a model reaching a ML R&D and Misalignment T/CCL.
paraphrase: This mitigation process applies to deployments of models reaching a ML R&D and Misalignment T/CCL.

excerpt: The approach is similar to misuse deployment mitigations, with an added focus on high-risk internal deployments.
paraphrase: This approach mirrors misuse deployment mitigations but adds attention to high-risk internal deployments.

excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
paraphrase: Safeguards and risk assessments are developed iteratively per the following steps.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability, which may include measures such as limiting affordances, monitoring and escalation, auditing, and alignment training, in addition to measures for preventing large-scale misuse.
paraphrase: Safeguards for ML R&D/misalignment may include limiting affordances, monitoring, escalation, auditing, and alignment training, plus misuse-prevention measures.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed in both internal and external deployment through testing (e.g. automated evaluations, red teaming) and threat modeling research. This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
paraphrase: Mitigation robustness for both internal and external deployment is assessed via testing and threat modeling, considering listed factors.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The effectiveness of the mitigations. For example, tests run on the safeguards may suggest that it is very unlikely they can be circumvented by external threat actors or the model in question.
paraphrase: Mitigation effectiveness is one factor, judged by whether tests suggest safeguards are hard to circumvent by threat actors or the model itself.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The likelihood and consequences of model misuse or misalignment, capability improvements after the risk assessment, and likelihood and consequences of our mitigations being circumvented, deactivated, or subverted.
paraphrase: Another factor is the likelihood and consequences of misuse or misalignment, capability change, and mitigation failure.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The scope of the deployment. For example, small-scale and private deployments may pose substantially less risk than large-scale or public deployments.
paraphrase: Deployment scope, such as scale and privacy, is a considered factor.

context_stem: This residual risk assessment could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: Model propensity for, historical incidence of and severity of related events: for example, such data may suggest a high (or low) likelihood of misalignment in or misuse of models at the T/CCL, and mitigations would consequently have to be stronger (or not as strong) for deployment to be appropriate.
paraphrase: Model propensity, historical incidence, and event severity inform how strong mitigations must be for the T/CCL.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying residual risk assessment are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Where the model has reached a CCL, the residual risk assessment will be supplemented with a safety case.
paraphrase: If a model reaches a CCL, the risk assessment is supplemented with a safety case.

excerpt: While the RAND framework is not specifically designed to address this case, we index it at present because it is the most useful reference in this area.
paraphrase: The RAND framework is used as a reference despite not being designed for this specific case, as it is currently the most useful option.

excerpt: See section 6 of https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01849.
paraphrase: A footnote points to section 6 of an external paper.

excerpt: Pre-deployment review of residual risk assessment: external deployments and high-risk internal deployments of a model take place only after the appropriate governance function determines the residual risk to be acceptable (including a safety case where a CCL has been reached).
paraphrase: External and high-risk internal deployment occur only after governance determines the residual risk acceptable, including a safety case if applicable.

context_stem: Pre-deployment review of residual risk assessment
excerpt: In particular, we will deem deployment mitigations adequate if the evidence suggests that for the T/CCLs the model has reached, the increase in likelihood of harm from the proposed deployment has been reduced to an acceptable level.
paraphrase: Mitigations are deemed adequate if evidence shows the harm-likelihood increase from deployment has been reduced acceptably.

excerpt: Post-deployment processes: our residual risk assessments, safety cases and mitigations may be updated as a result of post-market monitoring, including information about incidents relating to our frontier safety risk domains.
paraphrase: Post-deployment monitoring may prompt updates to risk assessments, safety cases, and mitigations.

excerpt: Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review and might result in updates to the related residual risk assessment or safety case.
paraphrase: Material safety case updates go to governance and may trigger further updates.

excerpt: This process is designed to ensure that residual risk remains at acceptable levels: evidence of efficacy collected during development and testing, as well as expert-driven estimates of other parameters, will enable us to assess residual risk and to detect substantial changes that invalidate our risk assessment.
paraphrase: This process aims to keep residual risk acceptable via efficacy evidence and expert estimates that flag invalidating changes.

excerpt: With iteration on mitigations and residual risk assessments, we believe that we are able to make informed decisions about the level of risk via a T/CCL before a model is deployed, and prevent models posing unacceptable levels of risk from being deployed.
paraphrase: Iteration is believed to enable informed pre-deployment risk decisions and prevent unacceptably risky deployments.

section_heading: 3.2 ML R&D and Misalignment Capability Levels
excerpt: We take a tiered approach to addressing ML R&D and misalignment risks:
paraphrase: A tiered approach is used to address ML R&D and misalignment risks.

section_heading: 3.2 ML R&D and Misalignment Capability Levels
context_stem: We take a tiered approach to addressing ML R&D and misalignment risks:
excerpt: We set a Stealth and Situational Awareness TCL that indicates a baseline level of model capability above which misalignment risks may begin to arise.
paraphrase: A Stealth and Situational Awareness TCL marks the baseline capability above which misalignment risks may emerge.

section_heading: 3.2 ML R&D and Misalignment Capability Levels
context_stem: We take a tiered approach to addressing ML R&D and misalignment risks:
excerpt: At this capability level we apply a proportionate set of mitigation and risk acceptance determination processes.
paraphrase: At the TCL threshold, a proportionate set of mitigations and risk acceptance processes applies.

section_heading: 3.2 ML R&D and Misalignment Capability Levels
context_stem: We take a tiered approach to addressing ML R&D and misalignment risks:
excerpt: We set ML R&D CCLs that indicate higher capability levels at which misalignment, misuse and structural risks are heightened and may reach a severe scale.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCLs mark higher capability levels where misalignment, misuse, and structural risks may become severe.

section_heading: 3.2 ML R&D and Misalignment Capability Levels
context_stem: We take a tiered approach to addressing ML R&D and misalignment risks:
excerpt: At these capability levels we apply a stronger set of mitigations, and follow the risk acceptance process as detailed in the rest of the framework.
paraphrase: At ML R&D CCLs, stronger mitigations apply and the full risk acceptance process described elsewhere is followed.

section_heading: 3.2.1 Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level
context_stem: The Stealth and Situational Awareness TCL is defined as follows:
excerpt: Stealth and Situational Awareness TCL: The instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness (ability to discover and use relevant details of its deployment setting) and stealth (ability to circumvent basic oversight mechanisms) such that, absent additional mitigations, we cannot rule out the model significantly undermining human control.
paraphrase: The TCL is defined as instrumental reasoning enabling enough situational awareness and stealth that, without extra mitigations, the model could undermine human control.

section_heading: 3.2.1 Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level
excerpt: When a model has reached this TCL, we will carry out periodic residual risk assessments of the misalignment risk posed.
paraphrase: Once the TCL is reached, periodic residual risk assessments of misalignment risk are conducted.

section_heading: 3.2.1 Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level
excerpt: This assessment may take into account models' alignment propensities, capabilities, and our defenses against misaligned models.
paraphrase: The assessment may consider alignment propensities, capabilities, and defenses against misaligned models.

section_heading: 3.2.1 Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level
excerpt: Since misalignment risks can manifest through internal use, these assessments will also account for the safety implications of high-risk internal deployments for such models.
paraphrase: Because misalignment risks can arise through internal use, assessments also cover the safety implications of high-risk internal deployments.

section_heading: 3.2.1 Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level
excerpt: If the risk assessment deems the residual risk from internal deployment to be unacceptable without additional safeguards (such as chain-of-thought monitoring on high-risk deployments), these will be applied.
paraphrase: If internal deployment risk is judged unacceptable without extra safeguards like chain-of-thought monitoring, those safeguards will be applied.

excerpt: We define ML R&D CCLs at capability levels at which misalignment, misuse and structural risks may reach a severe scale.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCLs are defined at capability levels where these risks may become severe.

excerpt: We expect these to evolve over time.
paraphrase: These CCLs are expected to change over time.

excerpt: We recommend a security level for each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
paraphrase: A recommended security level for each ML R&D CCL reflects the assessed minimum appropriate security for the field.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D acceleration level 1 / Critical Capability Level
context_stem: Row: ML R&D acceleration level 1; Column: Critical Capability Level
excerpt: ML R&D acceleration level 1: Has been used to accelerate AI development, resulting in AI progress substantially accelerating from historical rates.
paraphrase: ML R&D acceleration level 1 is defined as usage that substantially accelerates AI progress beyond historical rates.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D acceleration level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D acceleration level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: Security level 3 Unrestricted access to models at this level of capability could significantly increase a threat actor's ability to progress to yet more powerful models and other critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Security level 3 is recommended because unrestricted access could greatly boost a threat actor's ability to reach more powerful capabilities.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D acceleration level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D acceleration level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: The exfiltration of such a model may therefore have a significant effect on society's ability to adapt to and govern powerful AI models, effects that may have long-lasting consequences. Substantially strengthened security is therefore recommended.
paraphrase: Exfiltration could significantly and lastingly affect society's ability to govern powerful AI, justifying substantially strengthened security.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D acceleration level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D acceleration level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: However, we expect that acceleration will stem from systems of models integrated with workflows, rather than the model alone.
paraphrase: Acceleration is expected to come from integrated systems of models rather than a single model.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D acceleration level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D acceleration level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: The overall reduced impact of model weights counts against security levels with substantial innovation costs.
paraphrase: Because model weights alone have reduced impact, costly security levels are less justified here.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D automation level 1 / Critical Capability Level
context_stem: Row: ML R&D automation level 1; Column: Critical Capability Level
excerpt: ML R&D automation level 1: Can fully automate the work of any team of researchers at Google focused on improving AI capabilities, with approximately comparable all-inclusive costs.
paraphrase: ML R&D automation level 1 is defined as full automation of any Google AI capabilities research team at comparable cost.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D automation level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D automation level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: We recommend Security level 4 for this capability threshold, but emphasize that this must be taken on by the frontier AI field as a whole.
paraphrase: Security level 4 is recommended for this threshold, requiring field-wide adoption to be effective.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D automation level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D automation level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: Unrestricted access to models at this level of capability could give an actor (or AI systems) with adequate computational resources the ability to reach capabilities much more powerful than those in the other CCLs listed in a short amount of time.
paraphrase: Unrestricted access here could let a well-resourced actor or AI system reach much more powerful capabilities quickly.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D automation level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D automation level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: This could be catastrophic if there is no effective way of defending against rapidly improving and potentially superhuman AI systems wielded by threat actors.
paraphrase: Without effective defenses against rapidly improving, potentially superhuman AI, the outcome could be catastrophic.

section_heading: Table 3.2.2.a: ML R&D CCLs and Security Mitigations
locator: Table 3.2.2.a / ML R&D automation level 1 / Recommended security level and rationale
context_stem: Row: ML R&D automation level 1; Column: Recommended security level and rationale
excerpt: Therefore, we recommend models at this level of capability have exceptional security even though they may have substantial innovation costs.
paraphrase: Exceptional security is recommended at this level despite substantial innovation costs.

excerpt: The same caveats regarding security levels for misuse CCLs apply.
paraphrase: The caveats stated for misuse CCL security levels apply equally here.

excerpt: This level may include mitigations aligned with SL 2+, plus additional mitigations designed to prevent unilateral access, harden infrastructure, and prevent data exfiltration.
paraphrase: Security level 3 may add mitigations to prevent unilateral access, harden infrastructure, and prevent data exfiltration, beyond SL 2+.

paraphrase: Security level 4 may add measures to isolate model weights, enhance data center security, harden infrastructure, and minimize attack surface, beyond SL 2+ and 3.

excerpt: We have in place a well-established and comprehensive internal governance structure designed to ensure the robust implementation of the processes outlined in this Frontier Safety Framework.
paraphrase: A comprehensive internal governance structure is in place to ensure robust implementation of the Framework's processes.

excerpt: Responsibilities for assessing and mitigating risks are clearly defined and allocated across all levels of the organization.
paraphrase: Risk assessment and mitigation responsibilities are clearly assigned across all organizational levels.

excerpt: This includes legal, compliance, and safety reviews with escalation procedures to ensure appropriate oversight.
paraphrase: The governance structure includes legal, compliance, and safety reviews plus escalation procedures for oversight.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework will be reviewed at least once a year—more frequently if we have reasonable grounds to believe the adequacy of the Framework or our adherence to it has been materially undermined.
paraphrase: The Framework is reviewed at least annually, or more often if its adequacy or adherence is believed materially undermined.

excerpt: The process will involve (i) an assessment of the Framework's appropriateness for the management of significant and severe risk, drawing on information sources such as record of adherence to the framework, relevant high-quality research, information shared through industry forums, and evaluation results, as necessary, and (ii) an assessment of our adherence to the Framework.
paraphrase: The review process assesses the Framework's appropriateness using various information sources and separately assesses adherence to it.

excerpt: Following this assessment, we may:
paraphrase: Following the assessment, certain actions may be taken.

excerpt: Update our risk domains and T/CCLs, where necessary.
paraphrase: Risk domains and T/CCLs may be updated where necessary.

excerpt: Update our testing and mitigation approaches, where needed to ensure risk remains adequately assessed and addressed according to our current understanding.
paraphrase: Testing and mitigation approaches may be updated as needed to keep risk adequately assessed and addressed.

excerpt: The updated version and framework assessment will be reviewed by the appropriate corporate governance bodies.
paraphrase: Corporate governance bodies review the updated version and framework assessment.

excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share relevant information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate safety of frontier AI.
paraphrase: If a model reaches a CCL posing unmitigated material public-safety risk, relevant information is aimed to be shared with appropriate government authorities.

excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
paraphrase: Subject to confidentiality, security, and proprietary considerations, disclosed information may include certain items.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Model information: characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Disclosable information may include model characteristics relevant to the risk of its critical capabilities.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
paraphrase: Disclosable information may include evaluation design, results, and robustness test details.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
paraphrase: Disclosable information may include mitigation plan descriptions and their expected risk reduction.

excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organizations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
paraphrase: Disclosure to other external organizations may also be considered to promote shared learning and coordinated mitigation.

excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved over time.
